Healing skin doesn't rule out the complication. Waiting a month delays care for a kidney problem, and extra fluids aren't safe to push before anyone knows how the kidneys are working. More mupirocin treats the skin, not the kidneys.

Takeaway: Report dark urine, swelling, or low urine output after impetigo promptly.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how the nervous system is organized. Which of the following make up the central nervous system (CNS)?
options: The brain and the 12 pairs of cranial nerves
The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
The brain and the spinal cord
The spinal cord and the 31 pairs of spinal nerves
questions.rationale:
The brain and the spinal cord make up the CNS. The CNS receives and integrates information and sends out motor commands.

The other options include parts of the peripheral nervous system (PNS), which is everything outside the brain and spinal cord. The 12 pairs of cranial nerves and the 31 pairs of spinal nerves are peripheral nerves. The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions belong to the autonomic nervous system, which is part of the PNS.

questions.stem: For each body function, specify whether it is controlled mainly by the somatic nervous system or the autonomic nervous system.
rows: Speeding up the heart rate during exercise
Raising a hand to ask a question
Dilating the pupils in dim light
questions.rationale:
The somatic nervous system controls voluntary movement of skeletal muscles, such as walking and raising a hand.

The autonomic nervous system works automatically (involuntarily) on the heart, smooth muscle, and glands. Speeding up the heart rate, moving food through the intestines (peristalsis), dilating the pupils, and sweating are all automatic responses that a person doesn't consciously control.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how the peripheral nervous system carries information.
questions.text: Fibers that carry signals from sensory receptors toward the central nervous system are {{0}} fibers. Fibers that carry commands from the central nervous system to muscles and glands are {{1}} fibers. Voluntary movement of skeletal muscles is controlled by the {{2}} nervous system.
questions.rationale:
Afferent (sensory) fibers carry signals from receptors toward the CNS. Efferent (motor) fibers carry commands away from the CNS to muscles and glands. A memory aid: afferent arrives, efferent exits.

The somatic nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscle movement. The autonomic nervous system, including its parasympathetic division, works involuntarily on organs and glands. The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord, not a type of peripheral fiber.

questions.stem: Which part of a neuron receives most of the incoming signals from other neurons?
options: Axon terminal
Dendrites
Myelin sheath
Axon
questions.rationale:
Dendrites are the branching extensions of the neuron. They receive most of its input from other neurons and carry those impulses toward the cell body (soma).

The axon carries impulses away from the cell body, and the axon terminal at its end releases neurotransmitters to the next cell. The myelin sheath wraps and insulates the axon so impulses travel faster; it doesn't receive signals.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about the myelin sheath. Which of the following statements are accurate?
options: It speeds up the movement of action potentials along the axon.
Oligodendrocytes form it in the central nervous system.
It is a protective layer of fat (lipids) and protein.
Myelinated fibers make up the gray matter of the brain.
Schwann cells form it in the peripheral nervous system.
Damage to it makes nerve signals travel faster.
questions.rationale:
The myelin sheath is a protective layer of fat and protein wrapped around the axon. Like the insulation on an electrical wire, it speeds up the conduction of action potentials. Oligodendrocytes form myelin in the CNS, and Schwann cells form it in the PNS.

Myelinated fibers make up the white matter, not the gray matter; gray matter is mostly nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers. Damaged myelin slows nerve signals, or stops them altogether, as in multiple sclerosis.

questions.stem: For each type of neuroglia (glial cell), specify its main function.
columns: Acts as the brain's immune cell
Lines the ventricles and helps make cerebrospinal fluid
Forms myelin in the central nervous system
questions.rationale: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the brain and spinal cord, so they provide immune defense. Oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheath in the CNS. Astrocytes, the star-shaped glial cells, regulate the brain's internal environment, and their foot processes help form the blood–brain barrier. Ependymal cells line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord, and help produce cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.stem: Which glial cell is the most numerous in the central nervous system and helps regulate the brain's internal environment?
options: Schwann cell
Microglia
Satellite cell
Astrocyte
questions.rationale:
Astrocytes are the most numerous glial cells in the CNS. They regulate the brain's internal environment, including its energy supply and signal transmission, and their foot processes are part of the blood–brain barrier.

Microglia are the immune cells (macrophages) of the CNS. Satellite cells surround nerve cell bodies in peripheral ganglia, where they regulate the microenvironment much as astrocytes do in the brain. Schwann cells form myelin in the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: An action potential usually begins in which part of the neuron?
options: The dendritic tree
The nucleus of the cell body
The axon hillock
The myelin sheath
questions.rationale:
The axon hillock, where the axon leaves the cell body, has the most voltage-gated sodium channels. That makes it the most easily excited part of the neuron and the place where the action potential starts (the trigger zone).

Dendrites receive incoming signals and carry them toward the cell body. The nucleus in the cell body directs protein synthesis. The myelin sheath insulates the axon; it doesn't start impulses.

questions.stem: A client who has multiple sclerosis asks the nurse why the disease affects movement and sensation. The nurse should explain that multiple sclerosis damages which of the following?
options: The myelin sheath that insulates axons in the brain and spinal cord
The dopamine-producing neurons of the midbrain
The bones of the vertebral column
The sensory receptors in the skin
questions.rationale:
Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that causes inflammation and demyelination (loss of myelin) in the CNS, along with scarring (gliosis) and loss of neurons. Without myelin, nerve signals slow down or stop, so movement, sensation, and vision can all be affected.

Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the midbrain causes Parkinson disease. Multiple sclerosis doesn't damage the vertebrae or the skin's sensory receptors; it damages the nerve fibers that carry their signals.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how a neuron fires. Place the events of an action potential in the order in which they occur, starting with the neuron at rest.
items: The inside of the neuron rests at about −70 mV.
A stimulus brings the membrane to threshold.
Voltage-gated sodium channels open, and sodium rushes in (depolarization).
Potassium channels open, and potassium flows out (repolarization).
The membrane briefly becomes more negative than at rest (hyperpolarization).
The membrane returns to its resting potential.
questions.rationale: At rest, the inside of the neuron is about −70 mV. When a stimulus brings the membrane to threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium rushes in, so the inside becomes positive (depolarization, peaking near +30 mV). The sodium channels then close, and slower potassium channels open; potassium flows out and brings the charge back down (repolarization). Because the potassium channels close slowly, the membrane briefly overshoots the resting value (hyperpolarization) before it returns to rest. The refractory period during this time keeps the impulse moving in one direction.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the resting membrane potential of a neuron. Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: At rest, the inside of a neuron is {{0}} compared with the outside. Sodium ions are more concentrated {{1}} the cell, and the sodium-potassium pump moves {{2}}.

options: positive
negative
neutral
inside
outside
2 sodium ions out for every 3 potassium ions in
3 potassium ions out for every 2 sodium ions in
3 sodium ions out for every 2 potassium ions in

questions.rationale: At rest, the inside of a neuron is negative (about −70 mV) compared with the outside. Sodium is concentrated outside the cell, and potassium is concentrated inside. The sodium-potassium pump uses energy to move 3 sodium ions out for every 2 potassium ions in. This unequal exchange keeps the inside negative and maintains the concentration gradients the neuron needs to fire.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how action potentials work. Which statement describes the all-or-none principle?
options: A stronger stimulus produces a larger action potential.
An action potential travels in both directions along the axon at once.
A neuron can fire again immediately after an action potential.
Once threshold is reached, the action potential fires completely, at the same size every time.
questions.rationale:
Under the all-or-none principle, a stimulus that reaches threshold triggers a complete action potential, and a stimulus below threshold triggers none. A stronger stimulus doesn't make a bigger action potential; the size is always the same.

During the refractory period after an action potential, the sodium channels can't reopen, so the neuron can't fire again right away, and the impulse travels in only one direction down the axon.

questions.stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters are correctly matched with their functions?
options: GABA: the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain
Norepinephrine: slows the heart rate during rest
Dopamine: motor control, learning, and reward
Serotonin: the neurotransmitter lost in Parkinson disease
Acetylcholine: triggers skeletal muscle contraction at the neuromuscular junction
questions.rationale:
GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. Dopamine is involved in motor control, learning, reward, and emotion. Acetylcholine is released at the neuromuscular junction, where it triggers skeletal muscle contraction; it also helps regulate the heart, peristalsis, and gland secretion.

Norepinephrine carries sympathetic (fight-or-flight) responses, so it speeds up the heart; slowing the heart at rest is a parasympathetic effect of acetylcholine. Parkinson disease results from the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, not serotonin. Serotonin affects mood, bowel motility, bladder control, and cardiovascular function, and is linked to depression.

questions.stem: At the neuromuscular junction, which event directly causes the motor neuron to release acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft?
options: Sodium entering the muscle fiber
Calcium entering the nerve terminal
Acetylcholinesterase breaking down acetylcholine
Potassium leaving the muscle fiber
questions.rationale:
When an action potential reaches the motor neuron's terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open. Calcium entering the nerve terminal makes the vesicles fuse with the membrane and release acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft.

Acetylcholine then binds to receptors on the muscle fiber, and sodium enters the muscle fiber and depolarizes it; that happens after the release. Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine to end the signal. Potassium leaving a cell is part of repolarization, not neurotransmitter release.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the functions of the cerebral lobes. Click the lobe that contains the primary visual cortex.
questions.alt: Side view of the left side of a brain, with the front of the head on the viewer's left. Lines divide the cerebrum into four lobes. The cerebellum and brainstem are below the back of the cerebrum.
questions.rationale:
The occipital lobe, at the back of the cerebrum, contains the primary visual cortex. It receives information from the retina and interprets what the person sees.

The frontal lobe (front) handles voluntary movement, problem-solving, attention, memory, and speech production. The parietal lobe (top, behind the central sulcus) processes touch and body position. The temporal lobe (side, below the lateral sulcus) processes hearing and language comprehension. The cerebellum, below the occipital lobe, coordinates movement and balance.

questions.stem: Click the lobe that contains the auditory cortex, where hearing is processed.
questions.alt: Side view of the left side of a brain, with the front of the head on the viewer's left. Lines divide the cerebrum into four lobes. The cerebellum and brainstem are below the back of the cerebrum.
questions.rationale:
The temporal lobe, on the side of the brain below the lateral sulcus, contains the auditory cortex, which processes hearing. In the dominant hemisphere (usually the left), it also contains Wernicke's area, which is needed to understand language.

The occipital lobe processes vision, the parietal lobe processes touch and body position, and the frontal lobe controls voluntary movement and higher mental functions such as planning and judgment.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who had a stroke. The client speaks fluently, but the words make little sense, and the client can't follow spoken directions. The nurse should recognize that the stroke most likely damaged which area of the brain?
options: Broca's area in the frontal lobe
The primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe
Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe
The primary somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe
questions.rationale:
Wernicke's area, in the temporal lobe of the dominant hemisphere, is needed to understand spoken and written language. Damage to it leaves speech fluent but often meaningless, and the client can't follow directions.

Broca's area, in the frontal lobe, controls the muscles of speech; damage to it makes speech halting and effortful, while understanding is mostly kept. The visual cortex processes sight, and the somatosensory cortex processes touch and body position. Damage to these doesn't explain this client's language problem.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client who has damage to the cerebellum. Which finding should the nurse expect?
options: An unsteady, uncoordinated gait (ataxia)
Loss of the sense of smell
Inability to feel light touch on one side of the body
Inability to understand spoken words
questions.rationale:
The cerebellum coordinates smooth voluntary movement, balance, and motor learning. Damage to it causes ataxia (lack of coordination), poor balance, and an unsteady, abnormal gait.

The sense of smell depends on the olfactory nerve (CN I) and the olfactory area. Feeling light touch is processed in the somatosensory cortex of the parietal lobe. Understanding spoken words depends on Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe.

questions.stem: Which part of the brainstem regulates breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure, and coordinates the coughing, swallowing, and vomiting reflexes?
options: Pons
Midbrain
Thalamus
Medulla oblongata
questions.rationale:
The medulla oblongata, the lowest part of the brainstem, is continuous with the spinal cord. It regulates functions needed for survival: breathing (in response to carbon dioxide and pH), heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac contractility. It also coordinates protective reflexes such as vomiting, swallowing, coughing, and sneezing.

The pons relays signals between the cerebrum, cerebellum, and spinal cord. The midbrain is involved in movement and motivation, and its substantia nigra produces dopamine. The thalamus is part of the diencephalon, not the brainstem; it relays sensory information to the cortex.

questions.stem: Which functions does the hypothalamus regulate?
options: Body temperature
Smooth coordination of voluntary movement
Thirst and appetite
Hormone release by the pituitary gland
Relaying sensory information to the cerebral cortex
Sleep–wake (circadian) rhythms
questions.rationale:
Although small, the hypothalamus is essential for homeostasis. It regulates body temperature, thirst and appetite, heart rate, blood pressure, and circadian rhythms, and it links the nervous system to the endocrine system by controlling hormone release by the pituitary gland. It also makes antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin.

The cerebellum coordinates smooth voluntary movement. The thalamus is the main relay center that sends sensory information to the cerebral cortex.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client whose level of consciousness has decreased. The nurse recalls that which brain system keeps a person awake and alert?
options: The limbic system
The reticular activating system (RAS)
The basal nuclei
The cerebellum
questions.rationale:
The reticular activating system, part of the reticular formation in the brainstem, regulates consciousness. Sensory input keeps it active, which promotes wakefulness and alertness. It also filters out repetitive or unimportant stimuli, which prevents sensory overload.

The limbic system controls emotion, memory, and motivation. The basal nuclei help control voluntary movement and muscle tone. The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a cross-section of the spinal cord. Click an area of gray matter that contains the cell bodies of the motor neurons that control skeletal muscles.
questions.alt: Cross-section of the spinal cord, with the back (posterior) at the top and the front (anterior) at the bottom. Butterfly-shaped gray matter surrounds the central canal, and nerve roots with ganglia leave each side.
questions.rationale:
The cell bodies of the motor neurons that control skeletal muscles are in the ventral (anterior) horns of the gray matter: the broad lower wings of the butterfly in this view. Their fibers leave through the ventral roots to reach skeletal muscles.

The dorsal (posterior) horns, at the top, process incoming sensory information. Sensory fibers enter through the dorsal roots, and the cell bodies of those sensory neurons sit in the dorsal root ganglia, outside the cord. The white matter around the gray matter holds the ascending and descending tracts.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the protective layers around the spinal cord. Place the layers and spaces in order, starting at the vertebra and moving inward to the spinal cord.
questions.rationale: Just inside the bone of the vertebra is the epidural space, which holds fat (adipose tissue) and blood vessels. Next is the dura mater, the tough outer covering, then the subdural space. The arachnoid mater is the weblike middle layer. Beneath it, the subarachnoid space holds cerebrospinal fluid. The delicate pia mater clings directly to the surface of the spinal cord. A memory aid for the meninges from the outside in: DAP (dura, arachnoid, pia).

questions.stem: A nurse is assisting with a lumbar puncture to collect cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The nurse knows that the needle must reach which space?
options: The epidural space
The subdural space
The subarachnoid space
The central canal of the spinal cord
questions.rationale:
CSF circulates in the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, so that's where a lumbar puncture collects it. The needle goes in low in the lumbar spine, below the level where the spinal cord ends (around L1 to L2), so it doesn't touch the cord.

The epidural space lies outside the dura and holds fat and blood vessels, not CSF. The subdural space lies between the dura and the arachnoid. The central canal is inside the spinal cord itself, which a lumbar puncture must avoid.

questions.stem: How many pairs of spinal nerves branch from the spinal cord?
questions.rationale: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. Each one leaves the vertebral column through an opening between the vertebrae (the intervertebral foramen). Together with the 12 pairs of cranial nerves, they make up most of the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to test the cranial nerves that move the eyes. Which cranial nerves control eye movement?
options: Oculomotor (CN III)
Optic (CN II)
Trochlear (CN IV)
Facial (CN VII)
Abducens (CN VI)
Trigeminal (CN V)
questions.rationale:
Three cranial nerves move the eyes. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) moves most of the eye muscles, raises the eyelid, and constricts the pupil. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) moves the superior oblique muscle, which helps the eye look down. The abducens nerve (CN VI) moves the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward. A memory aid: LR6, SO4, and the rest are 3.

The optic nerve (CN II) carries vision, but it doesn't move the eye. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) carries sensation from the face and controls chewing. The facial nerve (CN VII) controls facial expression.

questions.stem: For each cranial nerve, specify whether it carries sensory signals, motor signals, or both.
questions.rationale:
The sensory nerves carry information to the brain: the olfactory nerve (CN I) for smell, the optic nerve (CN II) for vision, and the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) for hearing and balance. The motor nerves move muscles: the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) turns the head and shrugs the shoulders, and the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) moves the tongue. Two do both: the trigeminal nerve (CN V) carries facial sensation and controls the chewing muscles, and the facial nerve (CN VII) controls facial expression and carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue.

The memory aid Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More gives each nerve's type in order, from I to XII (S = sensory, M = motor, B = both).

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client's spinal accessory nerve (CN XI). Which instruction should the nurse give the client?
options: “Stick out your tongue and move it from side to side.”
“Clench your teeth while I feel your jaw muscles.”
“Smile, frown, and puff out your cheeks.”
“Shrug your shoulders and turn your head while I push against them.”
questions.rationale:
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles, so the nurse tests it by having the client shrug the shoulders and turn the head against resistance, and compares the strength of both sides.

Moving the tongue tests the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). Clenching the teeth tests the motor part of the trigeminal nerve (CN V). Smiling, frowning, and puffing out the cheeks test the facial nerve (CN VII).

questions.stem: A nurse notes that one side of a client's face droops when the client smiles, and the client reports that food tastes different on the front of the tongue. Which cranial nerve should the nurse suspect is affected?
options: Facial (CN VII)
Glossopharyngeal (CN IX)
Trigeminal (CN V)
Hypoglossal (CN XII)
questions.rationale:
The facial nerve (CN VII) controls the muscles of facial expression and carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue. It also controls the tear and saliva glands. Drooping on one side of the face with a change in taste points to this nerve.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries taste from the back third of the tongue and controls throat muscles. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) carries facial sensation and controls chewing. The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) moves the tongue.

questions.stem: Which of the following functions does the vagus nerve (CN X) control?
options: Slowing the heart rate
Turning the head
Movement of the throat and voice box muscles
Hearing and balance
Digestion, including motility of the stomach and intestines
Moving the tongue
questions.rationale:
The vagus nerve (CN X) is the main nerve of the parasympathetic nervous system. It controls organs in the chest and abdomen, so it slows the heart rate and supports digestion, and it moves the muscles of the throat and voice box for speech and swallowing.

Turning the head is controlled by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), hearing and balance by the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), and moving the tongue by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how a reflex works. Place the parts of a reflex arc in the order in which the signal passes through them.
questions.rationale: A reflex arc is a fast, automatic pathway. The receptor detects the stimulus; for a tendon reflex, the muscle spindle senses the stretch. The sensory (afferent) neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord. The integration center in the spinal cord connects it to the motor neuron, directly or through interneurons. The motor (efferent) neuron carries the command out, and the effector, a muscle or gland, responds.

questions.stem: A nurse taps the patellar tendon just below the kneecap with a reflex hammer. Which response should the nurse expect?
options: The hamstrings contract, and the knee bends.
The quadriceps contracts, and the lower leg kicks forward.
The foot points downward (plantar flexion).
The big toe moves up, and the other toes fan out.
questions.rationale:
Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps femoris, which reflexively contracts and extends the knee, so the lower leg kicks forward. This knee-jerk reflex is monosynaptic (one synapse between the sensory and motor neurons) and tests the femoral nerve and spinal segments L2 to L4.

The hamstrings bend the knee; this tap doesn't stretch them. Plantar flexion of the foot is the Achilles (ankle-jerk) reflex. The big toe moving up while the other toes fan out is the Babinski response, tested on the sole of the foot.

questions.stem: For each deep tendon reflex, specify the spinal cord segments it tests.
questions.rationale: Each deep tendon reflex tests a level of the spinal cord. The biceps reflex (musculocutaneous nerve) tests C5–C6. The triceps reflex (radial nerve) tests C7–C8. The patellar reflex (femoral nerve) tests L2–L4. The Achilles reflex (tibial nerve) tests S1–S2. The brachioradialis reflex (radial nerve) also tests C5–C6. An abnormal reflex helps locate a problem in the spinal cord or its nerves.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing the reflexes of a healthy 9-month-old infant. Which reflex is still expected at this age?
options: Moro (startle) reflex
Rooting reflex
Babinski reflex
Stepping reflex
questions.rationale:
The Babinski reflex (the big toe moves up and the other toes fan out when the sole is stroked) is normal in infants and is often present until about 12 months of age.

The other newborn reflexes fade much earlier: the Moro reflex by about 3 to 4 months, the stepping reflex by about 3 months, and the rooting reflex by about 4 to 6 months. A newborn reflex that lasts too long, or is missing or uneven, should be reported, because it can signal a problem in the central nervous system.

questions.stem: While supporting a newborn's head and neck, a nurse lets the newborn's body drop a few centimeters. The newborn's arms extend and spread outward, and the fingers open. How should the nurse document this response?
options: Moro (startle) reflex present
Tonic neck reflex present
Palmar grasp reflex present
Rooting reflex present
questions.rationale:
This is the Moro (startle) reflex: a sudden drop makes the newborn abduct and extend both arms, with the fingers opening. It's normal from birth and fades by about 3 to 4 months.

The tonic neck (fencing) reflex appears when the head is turned to one side: the arm on that side extends and the opposite arm flexes. The palmar grasp reflex is the newborn gripping a finger placed in the palm. The rooting reflex is turning toward the touch and opening the mouth when the cheek is stroked.

questions.stem: For each effect, specify whether it results from sympathetic or parasympathetic stimulation.
rows: The pupils constrict for near vision.
Blood flow to skeletal muscles increases.
The detrusor muscle contracts to empty the bladder.
Tear and saliva glands increase their secretions.
questions.rationale:
The sympathetic (fight-or-flight) division prepares the body for action: it dilates the bronchioles, increases blood flow to skeletal muscles, and makes the liver release glucose for energy.

The parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) division supports routine body functions: it constricts the pupils for near vision, increases gut motility, contracts the detrusor muscle (while relaxing the urethral sphincters) to empty the bladder, and increases tear and saliva secretion.

questions.stem: Which neurotransmitter do most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release at their target organs?
options: Acetylcholine
Dopamine
GABA
Norepinephrine
questions.rationale:
Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine, which activates adrenergic receptors on target organs. The adrenal medulla also releases epinephrine into the blood.

Acetylcholine is released by the preganglionic neurons of both divisions and by parasympathetic postganglionic neurons. Dopamine works mainly in the brain (motor control and reward), and GABA is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the two divisions of the autonomic nervous system.
questions.text: The sympathetic division is called the {{0}} system, and its preganglionic nerve cell bodies lie in the thoracic and upper lumbar spinal cord. The parasympathetic division is called the {{1}} system, and its fibers travel in cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X and in the sacral spinal nerves {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
The sympathetic division is the fight-or-flight system. Its preganglionic neurons start in the spinal cord from T1 to L2 (thoracolumbar). The parasympathetic division is the rest-and-digest system. Its fibers leave the brainstem in cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X, and leave the sacral spinal cord in the pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2 to S4 (craniosacral).

C5 to T1 and L1 to L5 aren't the outflow levels of either division, and “sense-and-respond” isn't a name for either one.

questions.stem: A client is having a strong sympathetic (fight-or-flight) response. Which findings should the nurse expect?
options: Dilated pupils
Constricted bronchioles
Increased heart rate
Increased urine output
Increased sweating
Decreased bowel sounds
questions.rationale:
The sympathetic response readies the body for action: the pupils dilate, the heart rate and contractility increase, sweat glands secrete more, and digestion slows, so bowel sounds decrease.

The bronchioles dilate, not constrict, to bring in more air. Urine output decreases, because the detrusor muscle relaxes and the urethral sphincters contract. Constricting the bronchioles and emptying the bladder are parasympathetic effects.

questions.stem: A client has Parkinson disease. The nurse recalls that the client's symptoms result from the loss of neurons that produce which neurotransmitter?
options: Acetylcholine
Dopamine
Serotonin
GABA
questions.rationale:
Parkinson disease is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, mainly in the substantia nigra of the midbrain. Dopamine is needed for smooth motor control, so clients develop movement problems such as a shuffling (parkinsonian) gait.

Acetylcholine works at the neuromuscular junction and in the parasympathetic system. Serotonin affects mood, sleep, and bowel function. GABA is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter.

questions.stem: For each finding, specify the term the nurse should use to document it.
rows: Lack of coordination of muscle movements
Can't carry out a learned movement when asked, even though strength is normal
Slurred speech caused by weak or poorly controlled speech muscles
questions.rationale: Dysphagia (dys = difficult, phagia = eating) is difficulty swallowing. Ataxia is a lack of coordination of muscle movements, often from damage to the cerebellum. Apraxia (a = without, praxis = action) is the inability to carry out a learned, purposeful movement even though the muscles work. Dysarthria (dys = difficult, arthr = articulation) is unclear speech caused by weakness or poor control of the muscles of speech, such as the tongue and lips.

questions.stem: During a mental status examination, a client says, “I feel hopeless.” The nurse observes that the client's facial expression doesn't change during the interview. How should the nurse document these findings?
options: Mood: flat. Affect: hopeless.
Thought process: hopeless. Thought content: flat.
Mood: hopeless. Affect: flat.
Insight: poor. Judgment: flat.
questions.rationale:
Mood is the client's own description of how they feel, so it's documented in the client's words: hopeless. Affect is the nurse's observation of the client's emotional expression; a face that doesn't change is a flat affect.

Thought process is how the client organizes their thoughts, and thought content is what they think about, such as suicidal thoughts or delusions. Insight is the client's understanding of their illness, and judgment is the ability to make sound decisions. A client who feels hopeless should also be asked directly about thoughts of suicide.

questions.stem: A nurse is giving a client the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Which tasks are part of this test?
options: Drawing a clock that shows 10 past 11
Reading an eye chart from 20 feet away
Subtracting 7 from 100, and continuing to subtract 7
Recalling a list of 5 words after a delay
Touching the nose with the eyes closed
Naming pictured animals, such as a lion and a camel
questions.rationale:
The MoCA screens cognition in several areas. It includes drawing a clock that shows 10 past 11 and copying a cube (visuospatial and executive function), naming animals (a lion, a rhinoceros, and a camel), serial sevens (subtracting 7 from 100 several times) and other attention tasks, repeating sentences, word fluency, abstraction, delayed recall of 5 words, and orientation.

Reading an eye chart tests vision and the optic nerve (CN II). Touching the nose with the eyes closed tests coordination (the cerebellum). Both belong to other parts of the neurological exam.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the neurological assessment of an older adult client. Click to highlight the findings that require follow-up.
questions.passage: [[Alert and oriented to person, place, and time]]. Speech is clear. [[Recalls 1 of 5 words after 5 minutes]]. [[Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light]]. [[Gait is wide-based and unsteady]], and [[client reports falling twice this month]]. [[Hand grips are strong and equal]].
questions.rationale:
The findings that need follow-up: recalling only 1 of 5 words after a delay suggests a memory problem that needs further cognitive assessment. A wide-based, unsteady gait and two falls this month show a high fall risk. Cognitive changes and falls are key concerns in older adults.

Being alert and oriented to person, place, and time, pupils that are equal, round, and reactive to light, and strong, equal hand grips are expected findings.

questions.stem: A nurse is using the BATHE technique to interview a client who is anxious about upcoming tests. Which question addresses the H in BATHE?
options: “What is going on in your life right now?”
“How is this affecting you?”
“What troubles you most about this situation?”
“How are you handling all of this?”
questions.rationale:
BATHE is a set of open-ended questions for brief, supportive interviews. H is Handling: “How are you handling it?”

“What is going on in your life?” addresses Background. “How is this affecting you?” addresses Affect. “What troubles you most?” addresses Troubles. BATHE ends with Empathy, a statement such as “That sounds very frustrating.”

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the 1900 nurses' note that show a change from the client's usual mental status.
questions.passage: Client is [[restless and pulling at the IV tubing]], and [[keeps asking where she is]]. Through the phone interpreter, the client [[does not know the day or the name of the hospital]], and [[has trouble following directions]]. [[Speech is clear]]. [[Hand grips are strong and equal]]. The daughter states that her mother [[lives alone and manages her own medications]], and that [[the confusion started this afternoon]].
questions.rationale:
The findings that show a change from baseline are new restlessness and pulling at the IV tubing, asking again and again where she is, not knowing the day or the hospital, and trouble following directions. Together they show new disorientation and inattention. The daughter's report that the confusion started this afternoon confirms that the change is sudden.

Clear speech and strong, equal hand grips are unchanged from 0800 and expected. That the client lives alone and manages her own medications describes her usual level of functioning (her baseline). It's what the nurse compares the current findings with, not a change.

questions.stem: For each finding, specify whether the client's status has improved, has not changed, or has declined since 0800.
questions.rationale:
Declined: orientation went from oriented to person, place, time, and situation to oriented to person only. The temperature rose from 37.6° C to 38.9° C, a new fever. And the client went from following directions to following them only with difficulty.

Improved: oxygen saturation rose from 91% on room air to 95% on 2 L/min of oxygen.

No change: the pupils are still equal, round, and reactive to light, and the hand grips are still strong and equal.

questions.stem: For each potential nursing action, specify whether it is indicated or not indicated for the client at this time.
rows: Use a professional medical interpreter to assess the client's orientation.
Ask the daughter to interpret the orientation questions.
Report the change in mental status to the provider right away, using SBAR.
Wait until morning to see whether the confusion clears.
Keep the bed low and the call light within reach, and check on the client often.
Give health information only to the daughter, as the daughter requested.
questions.rationale:
Indicated: a professional medical interpreter gives the most accurate assessment of orientation and cognition. A sudden change in mental status must be reported promptly; SBAR (situation, background, assessment, recommendation) organizes the report. A confused, restless client is at high risk for falls, so safety measures such as a low bed, the call light within reach, and frequent checks are needed.

Not indicated: family members shouldn't interpret assessment questions, because they may soften, add to, or answer for the client, which hides the true findings. Waiting until morning delays care for a sudden change that needs prompt reporting. The nurse can respect the family's cultural value of making decisions together, but shouldn't share information only with the daughter without knowing the client's own wishes. The nurse should ask the client, through an interpreter, how she wants her family involved, and support her autonomy.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: The client's findings are most consistent with {{0}}, because the confusion {{1}}. To judge this change, the nurse compares the client's current mental status with {{2}}.

options: dementia (a major neurocognitive disorder)
delirium (an acute confusional state)
expressive aphasia
a normal response to being in the hospital
has developed slowly over several years
affects only the ability to speak
began suddenly, along with a new fever
is expected in clients older than 75
her usual level of functioning, as described by her daughter
the average score for clients her age
the mental status of other clients on the unit
her expected mental status at discharge

questions.rationale:
The findings fit delirium, an acute confusional state. The confusion began suddenly (this afternoon), along with a new fever from the client's infection, and the client is newly disoriented, inattentive, and restless. Delirium needs prompt reporting, because its cause, such as an infection, can often be treated.

Dementia (a major neurocognitive disorder) develops slowly, over months to years, not in an afternoon. Expressive aphasia affects producing speech, and this client's speech is clear. Confusion is not a normal part of being in the hospital or of aging.

The best comparison is the client's own baseline: her daughter reports that she normally lives alone and manages her own medications. Averages for her age group or comparisons with other clients can't show a change in this client.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the client's findings at 1900.

options: Delirium
Dementia
Expressive aphasia
Cerebellar ataxia
Arrange a professional medical interpreter for assessments
Apply wrist restraints to protect the IV
Notify the provider of the change using SBAR
Have the daughter answer the assessment questions
Withhold oral fluids until the confusion clears
Orientation and attention
Babinski reflex
Temperature
Hearing in each ear
Deep tendon reflexes

questions.rationale:
The client's sudden confusion, inattention, and restlessness, with a new fever from an infection, point to delirium. Dementia develops slowly. Expressive aphasia affects producing speech, and her speech is clear. Cerebellar ataxia affects coordination, not thinking.

Actions: arrange a professional medical interpreter so assessments are accurate, and notify the provider using SBAR, because a sudden change in mental status needs prompt reporting. Restraints are a last resort and can increase agitation and injury. Family members shouldn't answer for the client or interpret assessments. Withholding fluids could cause dehydration, which can make delirium worse.

Parameters to monitor: orientation and attention, compared with her baseline, show whether the delirium is improving, and temperature tracks the infection that is its likely cause. The Babinski reflex, hearing, and deep tendon reflexes don't track this problem.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how a signal travels through a single neuron. Place the parts of the neuron in the order in which the signal passes through them.
questions.rationale:
A signal is received by the dendrites and carried to the soma (cell body), which holds the nucleus and combines the incoming signals. If they are strong enough, an action potential starts at the axon hillock, the trigger zone. The impulse travels down the axon, away from the soma, to the synaptic terminal, which releases neurotransmitters to signal the next cell.

Takeaway: Dendrite, soma, hillock, axon, terminal: dendrites detect, and axons send the signal away.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the glial cells of the peripheral nervous system. Which of the following cells control the microenvironment around the neurons of the sympathetic ganglia, much as astrocytes do in the CNS?
options: Ependymal cells
Satellite cells
Microglia
Oligodendrocytes
questions.rationale:
Satellite cells are glial cells of the peripheral nervous system. They surround the neuron cell bodies in ganglia, such as the sympathetic ganglia, and control their microenvironment, much as astrocytes do in the CNS.

Ependymal cells line the ventricles and the central canal and help make CSF, microglia are the CNS's resident macrophages, and oligodendrocytes make myelin in the CNS; all three are CNS cells.

Takeaway: The PNS glia are Schwann cells (myelin) and satellite cells (ganglia); the rest are CNS glia.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the charges of a neuron during an action potential. Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: A stimulus must raise the inside of the neuron to about {{0}}, the threshold, to start an action potential. At the peak of the action potential, the inside of the neuron reaches about {{1}}.

options: −90 mV
−55 mV
0 mV
+30 mV
−70 mV
+90 mV

questions.rationale:
At rest, the inside of a neuron is about −70 mV. A stimulus makes the inside less negative, and when it reaches about −55 mV, the threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and the action potential fires. Sodium rushing in carries the charge to a peak of about +30 mV, and then potassium flowing out brings it back down.

About −90 mV is in the range of hyperpolarization, below rest, and −70 mV is the resting potential, not the peak.

Takeaway: The resting potential is −70 mV, the threshold −55 mV, and the peak +30 mV, followed by hyperpolarization below −70 mV.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the hyperpolarization that follows repolarization. Which of the following describes its purpose?
options: It lets the neuron fire again right away, at a faster rate than before.
It makes the next action potential larger than the one before it.
It briefly stops the neuron from firing again, so the signal moves one way.
It opens the sodium channels again so that sodium can leave the cell.
questions.rationale:
After repolarization, the potassium channels close slowly, so the charge overshoots below −70 mV. During this refractory period, the neuron can't fire again right away, which keeps the impulse moving in one direction down the axon.

Hyperpolarization makes firing harder, not faster. Action potentials are all-or-none, so they don't grow larger. Sodium enters the cell during depolarization; it doesn't leave through sodium channels.

Takeaway: Hyperpolarization is the refractory period: it prevents immediate re-firing and keeps the signal moving one way.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how a neuron passes its message across a synapse. Place the events in order.
items: The impulse arrives at the presynaptic terminal.
The neurotransmitter crosses the synaptic cleft.
The neurotransmitter binds to receptors on the postsynaptic cell.
The neurotransmitter is broken down or taken back up, stopping the signal.
questions.rationale:
When the impulse reaches the presynaptic terminal, vesicles release the neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft, the gap between the cells. The neurotransmitter crosses the cleft and binds receptors on the postsynaptic cell, which changes that cell's chance of firing. Then the neurotransmitter is broken down or recycled, which stops the signal so that the next one comes through clearly.

Takeaway: Terminal, vesicles, cleft, receptors, and then the signal is stopped.

questions.stem: A client is given a medication that increases the effect of GABA at synapses in the brain. Which of the following effects should the nurse expect?
options: More excitement, because GABA makes neurons more likely to fire
A faster heart rate, because GABA is the main sympathetic neurotransmitter
Stronger muscle contractions, because GABA triggers skeletal muscle
Calming and drowsiness, because GABA makes neurons less likely to fire
questions.rationale:
GABA is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter. At an inhibitory synapse, it hyperpolarizes the next neuron and makes it less likely to fire, so boosting GABA's effect brings calming and drowsiness. The nurse watches for sedation and teaches fall safety.

An excitatory synapse makes the next neuron more likely to fire, which GABA doesn't do. The main sympathetic chemicals are norepinephrine and epinephrine, and acetylcholine triggers skeletal muscle contraction.

Takeaway: Excitatory synapses send the signal on; inhibitory synapses, such as those using GABA, hold it back.

questions.stem: A client has had a stroke and knows what to say but has great trouble forming the words. Click the lobe that contains Broca's area, which plans the movements of speech.
questions.alt: Side view of the left side of a brain, with the front of the head on the viewer's left. Lines divide the cerebrum into four lobes. The cerebellum and brainstem are below the back of the cerebrum.
questions.rationale:
Broca's area, in the frontal lobe (usually on the left), handles the motor planning for speech. When it is damaged, the client knows what to say but struggles to form the words. The frontal lobe also controls motor function, problem-solving, attention, memory, and language.

The parietal lobe processes touch and body position, the temporal lobe processes hearing, and the occipital lobe processes vision.

Takeaway: Broca's area, in the frontal lobe, plans the movements of speech.

questions.stem: With the eyes closed, a client can't tell which finger the nurse is touching or whether a toe is pointing up or down. Click the lobe that processes touch and body position.
questions.alt: Side view of the left side of a brain, with the front of the head on the viewer's left. Lines divide the cerebrum into four lobes. The cerebellum and brainstem are below the back of the cerebrum.
questions.rationale:
The parietal lobe processes sensation and proprioception: touch and body position. A client with parietal lobe damage may not be able to tell where a touch is, or where a body part is, without looking.

The frontal lobe handles movement, planning, and Broca's speech area, the temporal lobe hearing, and the occipital lobe vision. The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

Takeaway: The parietal lobe processes touch and body position.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the structures of the brain. For each function, click to specify the structure that performs it.
rows: Relays signals among the cerebrum, cerebellum, and spinal cord
Includes the hippocampus and the amygdala
Relays sensory information to the correct area of the cortex
Processes emotions such as compassion and empathy
Governs emotions, behavior, motivation, and memories
questions.rationale:
The thalamus is the relay center for sensory information: it sorts the signals and sends them to the right area of the cortex. The limbic system, which includes the hippocampus and amygdala, governs emotions, behavior, motivation, and memories, and influences the autonomic nervous system. The pons, in the hindbrain, relays signals among the cerebrum, cerebellum, and spinal cord. The insula, a lobe hidden deep inside the cerebrum, processes emotions such as compassion and empathy.

Takeaway: The thalamus relays sensation, the limbic system handles emotion and memory, the pons relays signals, and the insula holds empathy.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the surface of the cerebrum and the parts of the midbrain. Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: The ridges of the cerebral cortex are called {{0}}, and the grooves between them are called {{1}}. The dorsal (back) part of the midbrain is the {{2}}, and the {{3}} attach the cerebrum to the brainstem.

options: gyri
sulci
peduncles
gyri
sulci
ventricles
tegmentum
tectum
pons
cerebral peduncles
meninges
dorsal roots

questions.rationale:
The cerebral cortex, the brain's outer layer of gray matter, is folded into ridges called gyri (singular, gyrus) and grooves called sulci (singular, sulcus), which fit more cortex into the skull. In the midbrain, the tectum (Latin for roof) is the dorsal part, the tegmentum (covering, or floor) is the ventral part, and the cerebral peduncles are two stalks that attach the cerebrum to the brainstem.

Takeaway: Gyri are ridges and sulci are grooves; the tectum is the roof (dorsal) and the tegmentum the floor (ventral) of the midbrain.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the roots of the spinal nerves. For each description, click to specify the root it describes.
rows: Damage causes weakness but normal sensation in the area it serves
Carries sensory (afferent) signals into the spinal cord
Damage causes numbness but normal strength in the area it serves
Carries motor (efferent) commands out to the muscles
questions.rationale:
The dorsal (back) root carries sensory (afferent) signals into the cord, so damage to it causes numbness with normal strength. The ventral (front) root carries motor (efferent) commands out to the muscles, so damage to it causes weakness with normal sensation.

Takeaway: DAVE: dorsal is afferent (sensory), and ventral is efferent (motor).

questions.stem: A client has a subdural hematoma after a fall. Which of the following describes where the blood has collected?
options: Between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater
Between the skull and the dura mater
In the subarachnoid space, with the cerebrospinal fluid
Inside the pia mater, on the surface of the brain
questions.rationale:
The subdural space is the thin space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater, and that is where a subdural hematoma collects.

Blood between the skull and the dura is in the epidural space. The subarachnoid space, below the arachnoid, holds CSF. The pia mater is the delicate innermost layer, stuck to the brain; a hematoma doesn't collect inside it.

Takeaway: The epidural space is between bone and dura; the subdural space is between dura and arachnoid.

questions.stem: A client can't feel a wisp of cotton on the right cheek and has weakness when biting down, but can smile, frown, and raise the eyebrows normally. Which of the following cranial nerves is most likely affected?
options: Facial (CN VII)
Trigeminal (CN V)
Glossopharyngeal (CN IX)
Hypoglossal (CN XII)
questions.rationale:
The trigeminal nerve (CN V) carries facial sensation through its three branches (ophthalmic V1, maxillary V2, and mandibular V3) and controls the muscles for biting and chewing. Lost sensation on the cheek with a weak bite points to CN V.

The facial nerve (CN VII) controls facial expression, which is normal here; mixing up V and VII is a common error. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) serves the back of the tongue and the pharynx (taste, swallowing, and the gag reflex), and the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) moves the tongue.

Takeaway: Facial sensation and chewing are CN V; facial expression is CN VII.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client with a head injury. The client opens the eyes when the nurse speaks, says words that don't fit the conversation, and pulls the hand away when it is pinched. What is the client's Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
questions.rationale:
Add the three parts. Eye opening to a verbal command scores 3. A verbal response of inappropriate words scores 3. A motor response of withdrawing from pain scores 4. The total is 3 + 3 + 4 = 10, in the moderate range (9 to 12).

Common errors are scoring inappropriate words as confused (4), which is for a client who speaks in sentences but is disoriented, and scoring withdrawal as localizing (5), which means reaching toward the pain to push it away.

Takeaway: The GCS adds eyes (up to 4), verbal (up to 5), and motor (up to 6), for a score from 3 to 15.

questions.stem: A client's Glasgow Coma Scale score is 8. Which of the following classifications applies to this score?
options: Normal
Minor
Moderate
Severe
questions.rationale:
The GCS ranges from 3 to 15. A score of 8 or less is severe, 9 to 12 is moderate, and 13 or more is minor. A score of 8 means a severe injury, which the nurse reports right away.

A fully alert, oriented client who follows commands scores 15; a score of 8 is far below that.

Takeaway: A GCS of 8 or less is severe, 9 to 12 moderate, and 13 or more minor.

questions.stem: A client has a fever, a severe headache, a stiff neck, and sensitivity to light. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Start droplet precautions, and report the findings to the provider now.
Dim the lights, and recheck the client in 4 hours to see whether it passes.
Encourage the client to bend the neck forward several times to loosen it.
Give the client warm blankets, and offer fluids for the fever and chills.
questions.rationale:
Fever, a severe headache, a stiff neck (nuchal rigidity), and sensitivity to light point to meningitis, inflammation of the meninges. Bacterial meningitis is an emergency, so the nurse starts droplet precautions and reports the findings right away, so that testing and antibiotics can start fast.

Waiting 4 hours delays treatment of a possible emergency. Bending a stiff neck doesn't help and can hurt. Blankets and fluids don't address the cause. Encephalitis, inflammation of the brain itself, also causes fever and headache, with confusion or seizures.

Takeaway: Fever, a severe headache, and a stiff neck mean possible meningitis: start droplet precautions and report it right away.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the 2000 nurses' note that suggest rising intracranial pressure.
questions.passage: Client is [[restless and keeps trying to get out of bed]]. [[Opens the eyes only when the nurse speaks]], and [[is confused about where they are and why]]. [[Reports a worse headache]] and [[vomited once]]. [[Right pupil is larger than the left and reacts slowly to light]]. [[Lungs are clear]]. [[Skin is warm and dry]]. [[Moves all four extremities]].
questions.rationale:
Rising intracranial pressure (ICP) squeezes the brain. Its earliest sign is a change in level of consciousness: here, restlessness, eyes opening only to voice, and confusion, in a client who was alert and oriented at 1600. A worse headache, vomiting, and a larger, slow-reacting pupil are also signs of rising pressure.

Clear lungs, warm and dry skin, and moving all four extremities are expected findings.

Takeaway: In a head injury, a change in level of consciousness is the earliest sign of rising ICP, along with headache, vomiting, and pupil changes.

questions.stem: Using the 2000 nurses' note, what is the client's Glasgow Coma Scale score?
questions.rationale:
At 2000, the client opens the eyes to voice (3), is confused (4), and reaches toward the pinch to push it away, which is localizing (5): 3 + 4 + 5 = 12, in the moderate range. At 1600 the client was alert, oriented, and following commands, a GCS of 15, so the drop of 3 points is a decline that the nurse reports.

Scoring the motor response as following commands (6) doesn't fit, because the client no longer follows commands. Scoring the eyes as spontaneous (4) doesn't fit either, because the client opens them only when spoken to.

Takeaway: Score each part of the GCS from what the client does now, and report a drop.

questions.stem: Which of the client's findings is typically the earliest sign of increasing intracranial pressure?
options: The rise in blood pressure since 1600
The drop in heart rate since 1600
The change in level of consciousness
The larger right pupil that reacts slowly
questions.rationale:
The earliest sign of increasing intracranial pressure is a change in level of consciousness: restlessness, confusion, or drowsiness. That is why the nurse compares each neurological check with the last one.

A rising blood pressure, a slowing heart rate, and irregular breathing are late signs, and pupil changes usually come after the level of consciousness has changed. In this client, the blood pressure has risen to 146/72 and the heart rate has fallen to 66, so the pressure may be rising quickly.

Takeaway: A change in level of consciousness comes first; a higher blood pressure and slower heart rate come late.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
options: Lay the bed flat to increase blood flow to the brain.
Report the changes to the provider right away.
Recheck the client's neurological status in 4 hours.
Ask the provider for a sleep aid to calm the restlessness.
questions.rationale:
A falling level of consciousness, a worse headache, vomiting, a larger pupil, and a rising blood pressure with a slower heart rate are signs of rising intracranial pressure, an emergency. The nurse reports the changes right away, keeps the head of the bed raised about 30° with the head midline, and keeps checking.

Laying the bed flat can raise intracranial pressure further. Waiting 4 hours delays care for a worsening brain injury. A sleep aid would hide the changes in level of consciousness that the nurse needs to watch.

Takeaway: Signs of rising ICP are reported right away; keep the head of the bed at about 30°, with the head midline.

questions.stem: At 2030, the client has a seizure. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Note the time the seizure starts.
Place a bite block in the client's mouth.
Turn the client onto the side.
Hold the client's arms down to stop the jerking.
Protect the client's head from injury.
Loosen any tight clothing.
questions.rationale:
During a seizure, a sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain, safety comes first: the nurse times the seizure, protects the head, turns the client onto the side so that saliva drains and the airway stays open, and loosens tight clothing. Afterward, the client may be drowsy and confused (post-ictal).

The nurse puts nothing in the mouth: a bite block can break teeth or block the airway. And the nurse doesn't restrain the client, because holding the limbs down can cause injury.

Takeaway: During a seizure, time it, protect the head, turn the client on the side, and loosen clothing; put nothing in the mouth, and don't restrain.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the senses. For each sense, click to specify whether it is a general sense or a special sense.
questions.rationale: General senses use receptors spread throughout the body: touch, pressure, pain, temperature, proprioception (the position of body parts and the effort used to move them), and interoception (the body's internal condition). Special senses have specialized sense organs: vision (the eyes), hearing and equilibrium (the inner ear), taste (taste buds), and smell (olfactory receptors).

questions.stem: With the client's eyes closed, a nurse moves the client's big toe up, then down, and asks which way it moved. Which sense is the nurse testing?
options: Interoception
Vestibular sense
Proprioception
Nociception
questions.rationale:
Proprioception is the awareness of where body parts are in relation to each other, and of the effort used to move them. Asking a client to say which way a toe or finger was moved, with the eyes closed, tests it.

Interoception is awareness of the body's internal condition, such as hunger, thirst, or a full bladder. The vestibular sense detects the movement and position of the head relative to gravity, for balance. Nociception is the detection of pain by nociceptors.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing sensory receptors. For each receptor, click to specify the stimulus it detects.
columns: Oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH of the blood
questions.rationale: Rods and cones are photoreceptors in the retina that convert light into nerve signals. The carotid and aortic bodies are chemoreceptors that monitor the blood's oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH. Free nerve endings act as nociceptors, which detect pain, and as thermoreceptors. Olfactory receptor neurons are chemoreceptors in the nose that respond to odor molecules.

questions.stem: A client steps on a tack and feels an immediate, sharp pain, followed a moment later by a dull ache. What is the immediate, sharp pain called?
options: Slow (second) pain
Referred pain
Fast (first) pain
Visceral pain
questions.rationale:
Fast pain, also called first pain, is the immediate, sharp, well-localized pain felt when the skin is pricked or cut. Slow pain, or second pain, is the delayed, dull ache that follows, like the ache after stubbing a toe.

Referred pain is felt at a site different from where it starts, such as arm pain during a heart attack. Visceral pain comes from internal organs and is usually hard to pinpoint.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing why some medications cause nausea. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The chemoreceptor trigger zone, located in the {{0}}, responds to drugs and hormones in the blood and can cause {{1}}.

options: cerebellum
occipital lobe
medulla
coughing
vomiting
fever

questions.rationale:
The chemoreceptor trigger zone sits in the medulla of the brainstem. It responds to drugs and hormones carried in the blood and can trigger nausea and vomiting, which is why some medications cause nausea.

The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance, and the occipital lobe interprets vision. The trigger zone doesn't cause coughing, a reflex set off by irritation of the airway, or fever, which the hypothalamus regulates.

questions.stem: A client runs the fingertips over a piece of fabric to feel its fine texture. Which receptors, concentrated in the hairless skin of the fingertips, make this possible?
options: Meissner corpuscles
Pacinian corpuscles
Ruffini endings
Free nerve endings
questions.rationale:
Meissner corpuscles lie in the dermal papillae of hairless (glabrous) skin, such as the fingertips, and sense light touch and fine movement across the skin, like the texture of fabric.

Pacinian corpuscles sense high-frequency vibration and deep pressure. Ruffini endings sense stretch, sliding of the skin, and changes in joint angle. Free nerve endings detect pain and temperature.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching about the visceral senses. Which sensations are visceral senses?
options: Hearing music
Nausea
Seeing the color red
The need to urinate
Thirst
Hunger
questions.rationale:
Visceral senses tell the brain about the internal organs and the body's needs: nausea, hunger, thirst, and the need to urinate or defecate. They are part of interoception, the awareness of the body's internal condition.

Seeing a color (vision) and hearing music (hearing) are special senses, which use specialized sense organs to detect stimuli from outside the body.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how tears are made and drained. Place the steps in order.
items: Blinking spreads the tears across the surface of the eye.
The tears drain into the lacrimal puncta near the inner corner of the eye.
The tears collect in the lacrimal sac.
The tears drain through the nasolacrimal duct into the nose.
questions.rationale: Tears are made in the lacrimal glands, almond-sized glands at the upper outer corner of each eye. Blinking spreads the tears across the eye, where they mix with oil from the meibomian glands. Used tears drain through the lacrimal puncta, small openings in the upper and lower lids near the nose, into the lacrimal sac in the inner corner, and then through the nasolacrimal duct into the nose. That's why the nose runs when a person cries.

questions.stem: A client has dry eyes because the tears evaporate too quickly. Which structures normally add oil to the tears to slow evaporation?
options: Lacrimal glands
Lacrimal puncta
Conjunctiva
Meibomian glands
questions.rationale:
The meibomian glands, along the edges of the eyelids, make oil that mixes with the watery tears. The oil slows evaporation, helps the tears cling to the eye, and keeps them from spilling over the lashes.

The lacrimal glands make the watery, salty part of the tears, which cleans and lubricates the eye and is antiseptic. The lacrimal puncta drain used tears away. The conjunctiva is a thin mucous membrane over the sclera.

questions.stem: Which statement about the conjunctiva is accurate?
options: It is the colored part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil.
It is the clear dome at the front of the eye that bends light.
It produces the watery part of the tears.
It is a thin mucous membrane that covers the sclera but not the cornea.
questions.rationale:
The conjunctiva is a thin, protective mucous membrane that covers the sclera (the white of the eye) and lines the eyelids. It does not cover the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye.

The iris is the colored part that controls the pupil. The cornea is the clear dome that bends light as it enters. The lacrimal glands produce the watery part of the tears.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the structures of the eye. For each structure, click to specify its function.
columns: Bends light as it enters the eye
Controls the size of the pupil
questions.rationale: The cornea, the clear front part of the outer layer, bends (refracts) light as it enters. The iris, the colored part, controls the size of the pupil and so the amount of light let in. The lens, controlled by the ciliary muscles, becomes thicker or thinner to focus light on the retina. The retina lines the back of the eye; its rods and cones convert light into nerve impulses, which leave the eye through the optic nerve. The choroid is the layer that carries the eye's blood supply.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the anatomy of the eye. Click the structure that changes thickness to focus on objects at different distances.
questions.alt: Side view of the eye with the front on the left: a clear dome at the front, the colored iris with an opening in the middle, a clear oval structure behind the opening, a jelly-filled chamber lined by layers at the back, a small yellow spot at the center of the back, and a thick nerve leaving the back of the eye.
questions.rationale:
The lens, the clear oval structure just behind the pupil, focuses light on the retina. The ciliary muscles change its thickness: it becomes thicker and rounder to focus on near objects (accommodation) and thinner for distant ones. Clouding of the lens is a cataract.

The cornea, the clear dome at the front, bends light but doesn't change shape to focus. The macula, the yellow spot at the back, gives sharp central vision. The optic nerve carries signals from the retina to the brain.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the fluids of the eye.
questions.text: The {{0}} humor fills the space in front of the lens and bathes the iris and pupil. The {{1}} humor is a clear, jellylike substance that fills the large cavity behind the lens.
questions.rationale:
The aqueous humor is a watery fluid that fills the anterior and posterior chambers, in front of the lens, and bathes the iris, pupil, and lens. The vitreous humor is a clear, jellylike substance that fills the cavity behind the lens and helps the eye keep its shape.

Lacrimal fluid is tears, which bathe the outside of the eye. Serous fluid is the thin, watery fluid made by serous membranes, such as those lining the chest and abdomen; it isn't one of the humors of the eye.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching how light becomes vision. Place the structures in the order in which light, and the signals it creates, pass through them.
questions.rationale: Light enters through the cornea, which bends it, passes through the pupil, whose size the iris controls, and is focused by the lens onto the retina. The retina's rods and cones convert the light into electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve (cranial nerve II) to the occipital lobe, where the visual cortex interprets them.

questions.stem: For each statement, click to specify whether it describes rods or cones.
rows: Most densely packed in the fovea centralis
questions.rationale: Rods work in low light and are mainly responsible for night vision. Cones work in bright light and perceive color, with red, green, and blue cones. The fovea centralis, a small pit at the center of the macula, is packed with cones, which is why it gives the sharpest central vision.

questions.stem: Click the area of the retina that is responsible for sharp central vision.
questions.alt: Side view of the eye with the front on the left: a clear dome at the front, the colored iris with an opening in the middle, a clear oval structure behind the opening, a jelly-filled chamber lined by layers at the back, a small yellow spot at the center of the back, and a thick nerve leaving the back of the eye.
questions.rationale:
The macula is the central part of the retina, at the back of the eye. At its center is the fovea centralis, a small pit packed with cones, which gives the sharpest central vision. Macular degeneration damages this area and causes loss of central vision.

The lens focuses light, the optic nerve carries signals to the brain, and the rest of the retina, which has more rods, supports side (peripheral) and night vision.

questions.stem: A client looks up from a book to a sign across the room, then back at the book. Which change lets the eyes focus on the book again?
options: The lens becomes thinner and flatter.
The cornea changes shape.
The lens becomes thicker and rounder.
The pupils dilate.
questions.rationale:
Accommodation is the eye's response for focusing on near objects. The ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens: it becomes thicker and rounder, which bends light more and focuses the near image on the retina. The pupils also constrict.

A thinner, flatter lens focuses on distant objects. The cornea bends light but doesn't change shape to focus. The pupils constrict, not dilate, when focusing up close.

questions.stem: Click the structure that carries visual impulses from the retina to the brain.
questions.alt: Side view of the eye with the front on the left: a clear dome at the front, the colored iris with an opening in the middle, a clear oval structure behind the opening, a jelly-filled chamber lined by layers at the back, a small yellow spot at the center of the back, and a thick nerve leaving the back of the eye.
questions.rationale:
The optic nerve (cranial nerve II) leaves the back of the eye and carries impulses from the retina's rods and cones to the brain, where the occipital lobe interprets them.

The lens focuses light, the macula is the area of the retina for sharp central vision, and the cornea bends light as it enters the eye. None of them carries signals to the brain.

questions.stem: A nurse is screening a client's visual acuity. Which tool should the nurse use?
options: Tuning fork
Otoscope
Snellen chart
Reflex hammer
questions.rationale:
Visual acuity, how clearly a person sees, is tested with a Snellen chart, a wall chart of letters that get smaller on each line.

A tuning fork is used to assess hearing, an otoscope to examine the ear canal and eardrum, and a reflex hammer to test deep tendon reflexes.

questions.stem: For each eye disorder, click to specify its description.
columns: Loss of central vision from damage to the macula
Damage to the retina's small blood vessels from long-term high blood glucose
Loss of side vision from increased pressure in the eye
questions.rationale: A cataract is clouding of the lens, as its proteins break down and clump, causing blurred or dim vision. Glaucoma involves increased intraocular pressure that damages the optic nerve and causes loss of peripheral (side) vision. Macular degeneration damages the macula, causing loss of central vision, mostly in people over 50. Diabetic retinopathy is damage to the retina's small blood vessels from long-term high blood glucose, and it can lead to blindness.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client who has no vision problems asks why regular eye exams are needed. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: Glaucoma can damage vision before a person notices any symptoms.
Cataracts always cause eye pain, so exams aren't needed until pain begins.
Aging affects only the ability to see colors.
Eye exams are needed only for people who wear glasses.
questions.rationale:
Glaucoma often causes no symptoms at first, and more than half of the people who have it don't know it. Regular eye exams can find raised intraocular pressure and early damage before vision is lost. Diabetic retinopathy is also silent early on.

Cataracts cause gradual clouding and blurred vision, not pain. Aging affects more than color vision: cataracts, macular degeneration, and glaucoma all become more common. Eye exams matter for everyone, not only people who wear glasses.

questions.stem: A client can read a book clearly but can't read road signs while driving. The nurse recognizes this as which condition?
options: Hyperopia (farsightedness)
Myopia (nearsightedness)
Macular degeneration
Strabismus
questions.rationale:
Myopia (nearsightedness) is a refractive error in which near objects are clear but distant objects are blurry, because the eye focuses distant images in front of the retina.

Hyperopia (farsightedness) is the opposite: distant objects are clearer than near ones. Macular degeneration causes loss of central vision at any distance. Strabismus is misalignment of the eyes.

questions.stem: During a well-child visit, a nurse notices that one of a 4-year-old child's eyes turns inward. Why should the nurse refer the child for an eye exam?
options: The eye will straighten as the child grows, so the referral can wait until age 10.
An eye that turns inward is a sign of glaucoma.
Strabismus affects only how the eyes look, not how the child sees.
Untreated misalignment of the eyes can lead to amblyopia and loss of binocular vision.
questions.rationale:
An eye that turns inward (esotropia) is a form of strabismus, misalignment of the eyes. Early treatment matters, because untreated strabismus can lead to amblyopia (reduced vision in one eye), loss of binocular vision, and double vision.

Strabismus doesn't reliably go away with growth, so waiting risks permanent vision loss. It isn't a sign of glaucoma. It affects how the child sees, not just how the eyes look.

questions.stem: When a nurse shines a light into a client's right eye, both pupils constrict. Which cranial nerve carries the signal that makes the pupils constrict?
options: Optic nerve (cranial nerve II)
Oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III)
Trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV)
Abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI)
questions.rationale:
In the pupillary light reflex, the optic nerve (CN II) carries the light signal from the retina to the brain, and the oculomotor nerve (CN III) carries the command back to the muscles of the iris, which constrict both pupils. Checking the direct and consensual responses helps show whether a problem lies with CN II or CN III.

The optic nerve senses the light but doesn't constrict the pupil. The trochlear (CN IV) and abducens (CN VI) nerves move the eye but don't control the pupil.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching how sound is heard. Place the steps in order.
items: Sound waves travel through the external auditory canal.
The sound waves vibrate the tympanic membrane.
The malleus, incus, and stapes vibrate.
The stapes pushes on the oval window, moving the fluid in the cochlea.
Hair cells in the cochlea change the movement into nerve signals.
The vestibulocochlear nerve carries the signals to the brain.
questions.rationale: Sound waves enter the outer ear and travel through the ear canal to the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which vibrates. The vibration passes through the three ossicles of the middle ear, the malleus, incus, and stapes. The stapes pushes on the oval window, creating pressure waves in the fluid of the cochlea, where hair cells of the organ of Corti turn the movement into nerve signals. The signals travel along the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) to the brain's hearing center.

questions.stem: Click the structure in which hair cells change fluid vibrations into nerve signals.
questions.alt: Cross-section of the ear with the outside of the head on the left: the outer ear, a canal leading to a thin membrane, an air-filled space with three tiny bones, a tube running down from that space, three looped canals, a small chamber below them, and a snail-shaped spiral, with a nerve leading toward the brain.
questions.rationale:
The cochlea, the snail-shaped spiral of the inner ear, contains the organ of Corti. Its hair cells change fluid waves into nerve signals, which travel to the brain along the vestibulocochlear nerve. Damage here causes sensorineural hearing loss.
