The semicircular canals, the three loops above it, sense rotation of the head for balance. The middle ear, the air-filled space with the three tiny bones, passes vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear. The ear canal carries sound waves to the eardrum.

questions.stem: A client asks why the ears “pop” as an airplane descends. Which structure equalizes the pressure in the middle ear with the throat?
options: Cochlea
Semicircular canals
External auditory canal
Eustachian tube
questions.rationale:
The eustachian tube connects the air-filled middle ear to the nasopharynx, so the pressure in the middle ear can equalize with the pressure in the throat. When it opens during swallowing or yawning, the ears “pop.” A swollen eustachian tube can trap fluid in the middle ear, which can lead to otitis media.

The cochlea changes fluid vibrations into nerve signals for hearing. The semicircular canals sense head rotation for balance. The external auditory canal carries sound to the eardrum; it's outside the eardrum and doesn't open into the middle ear.

questions.stem: A client asks whether earwax is harmful and should be removed every day. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: Earwax protects the ear canal, but too much can block it and muffle hearing.
Earwax is a sign of an ear infection and should be removed every day.
Earwax is made by the cochlea to protect the hair cells inside the ear.
Earwax has no purpose, so removing all of it every day is healthiest.
questions.rationale:
Cerumen (earwax), made by ceruminous glands in the ear canal, cleans and lubricates the canal and has antimicrobial properties. But too much cerumen, or an impaction, can block the canal and cause conductive hearing loss, so the nurse checks for cerumen during a hearing assessment.

Earwax is normal, not a sign of infection, and doesn't need daily removal. It's made in the ear canal, not the cochlea. It has a purpose, so removing all of it isn't healthiest.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing a hearing assessment. Which information should the nurse gather?
options: How effectively the client communicates
Whether cerumen is blocking the ear canals
Whether the client can taste salt on the tongue
The client's ability to read a Snellen chart
How well the client hears normal conversation
Whether the client uses hearing aids
questions.rationale:
A hearing assessment focuses on hearing acuity, whether the client uses hearing aids, any cerumen that could block sound, and how effectively the client communicates. The findings help the nurse tell conductive from sensorineural hearing loss and adapt how they communicate with the client.

The Snellen chart tests visual acuity, and taste is tested when assessing cranial nerves VII and IX, not hearing.

questions.stem: Click the structures that sense rotation of the head to help keep the body balanced.
questions.alt: Cross-section of the ear with the outside of the head on the left: the outer ear, a canal leading to a thin membrane, an air-filled space with three tiny bones, a tube running down from that space, three looped canals, a small chamber below them, and a snail-shaped spiral, with a nerve leading toward the brain.
questions.rationale:
The semicircular canals, the three looped canals of the inner ear, detect rotation of the head. With the vestibule, they send signals along the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) that help maintain balance, posture, and steady vision. Problems here can cause vertigo and falls.

The cochlea, the spiral below them, is for hearing. The middle ear passes sound vibrations to the inner ear. The ear canal carries sound to the eardrum.

questions.stem: A child has acute otitis media. Click the space where the fluid collects.
questions.alt: Cross-section of the ear with the outside of the head on the left: the outer ear, a canal leading to a thin membrane, an air-filled space with three tiny bones, a tube running down from that space, three looped canals, a small chamber below them, and a snail-shaped spiral, with a nerve leading toward the brain.
questions.rationale:
In acute otitis media, viruses or bacteria grow in fluid trapped in the middle ear, the air-filled space just behind the eardrum that holds the three tiny bones. A swollen eustachian tube can keep the fluid from draining, causing ear pain and muffled hearing (a conductive hearing loss).

The ear canal is outside the eardrum; an infection there is otitis externa. The cochlea and semicircular canals are parts of the inner ear.

questions.stem: For each ear disorder, click to specify its description.
columns: Gradual hearing loss in both ears with aging
Ringing or buzzing that usually only the client can hear
Episodes of vertigo, changing hearing loss, tinnitus, and a full feeling in the ear
Infection with fluid trapped in the middle ear
questions.rationale: Acute otitis media is an infection of fluid trapped in the middle ear, causing ear pain and muffled hearing. Presbycusis is the gradual, bilateral hearing loss of aging. Tinnitus is a high-pitched ringing or buzzing that is usually heard only by the client. Ménière disease is a chronic inner ear disorder, thought to come from excess fluid in the inner ear, with episodes of vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a feeling of fullness in the ear.

questions.stem: A client reports that the room seems to spin when the client rolls over in bed. Which term should the nurse use to document this symptom?
options: Tinnitus
Presyncope
Vertigo
Proprioception
questions.rationale:
Vertigo is a false sense of motion, of oneself or the surroundings, often spinning. It usually comes from the vestibular system, as in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which is set off by changes in head position.

Tinnitus is ringing or buzzing in the ears. Presyncope is the lightheaded feeling of being about to faint, not spinning. Proprioception is the sense of body position, not a symptom.

questions.stem: A client with Ménière disease has sudden episodes of vertigo. Which action is the nurse's priority?
options: Encourage the client to keep walking until the episode passes.
Help the client sit or lie down to prevent a fall.
Schedule a hearing test for later in the week.
Teach the client to follow a low-sodium diet.
questions.rationale:
Vertigo affects balance and posture, so safety comes first: during an episode, the nurse helps the client sit or lie down, keeps the call light within reach, and helps with walking afterward to prevent falls.

Walking during vertigo increases the risk of falling. A hearing test is useful, since Ménière disease affects hearing, and a low-sodium diet can help reduce episodes over time, but neither comes first while the client is dizzy.

questions.stem: For each basic taste, click to specify the substance that produces it.
questions.rationale: Sweet tastes come from sugars and sweeteners, sour from free hydrogen ions (acids), salty from sodium ions, bitter from alkaloids, and umami (savory) from glutamate and other amino acids. Ion channels detect salty and sour tastes, and G protein-coupled receptors detect sweet, bitter, and umami.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the cranial nerves that carry taste. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: Taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue travels to the brain on cranial nerve {{0}}, and taste from the back one-third travels on cranial nerve {{1}}.

options: VII (facial)
IX (glossopharyngeal)
X (vagus)
VII (facial)
IX (glossopharyngeal)
X (vagus)

questions.rationale: Taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue travels on the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). Taste from the back one-third of the tongue and the rest of the mouth travels on the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Taste receptors in the back of the throat and the esophagus send signals on the vagus nerve (CN X).

questions.stem: Place the steps of the sense of smell in order.
items: Odor molecules bind to receptors on olfactory sensory neurons in the nose.
The neurons send signals through the cribriform plate.
The signals reach the olfactory bulb.
The signals travel along the olfactory tract.
The olfactory center of the brain interprets the smell.
questions.rationale: Smell starts when odor molecules bind to receptors on olfactory sensory neurons, which fire signals along the olfactory nerves through the cribriform plate of the skull to the olfactory bulb. From there, the signals travel along the olfactory tract to the olfactory center of the brain. Its connections to the limbic system tie smells to emotions and memories.

questions.stem: An older adult reports that food has little taste or smell. Which risks should the nurse address?
options: A stronger desire to eat
Better hearing and vision
Not noticing smoke or a gas leak
Eating spoiled food without noticing
Poor appetite and weight loss
questions.rationale:
Smell and taste work together to create flavor, so their loss can reduce appetite and affect nutrition. Smell also protects safety: the client may not notice smoke, a gas leak, or spoiled food. The nurse can suggest working smoke and gas detectors, checking the dates on food, and making meals more appealing with color and texture.

Losing smell and taste doesn't improve hearing or vision, and it usually reduces, rather than increases, the desire to eat.

questions.stem: A client with a stuffy nose from a cold says that food has lost its flavor. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: Smell is part of flavor, so a blocked nose dulls the taste of food.
The cold virus has permanently damaged the client's taste buds.
Flavor depends only on the taste buds on the tongue, not the nose.
Taste signals travel to the brain on the olfactory nerve.
questions.rationale:
Taste is a multisensory experience: smell, texture, and taste work together to create flavor. When congestion keeps odor molecules from reaching the olfactory receptors, food seems to have little flavor, even though the taste buds still work.

A cold doesn't permanently damage the taste buds. Flavor does not depend only on the tongue. Taste travels on cranial nerves VII, IX, and X; the olfactory nerve carries smell.

questions.stem: For each description of pain, click to specify the type of pain.
rows: Burning, shooting pain in the feet from diabetic nerve damage
Pain in the left arm and jaw during a heart attack
Cramping pain from the intestines that is hard to pinpoint
Sharp, well-localized pain from a cut on the hand
questions.rationale: Somatic pain, a type of nociceptive pain, comes from nociceptors in the skin or deep tissues and is usually well localized, like a cut. Visceral pain, also nociceptive, comes from internal organs and is often cramping and hard to pinpoint. Neuropathic pain comes from a problem in the nervous system itself, such as diabetic nerve damage, and is often burning or shooting. Referred pain is felt at a site different from its source, such as arm and jaw pain from the heart.

questions.stem: A client who had surgery yesterday rates the pain as 8 on a scale of 0 to 10 while calmly reading a book. Which is the most reliable indicator of the client's pain?
options: The client's calm facial expression
The client's report of the pain
The client's vital signs
The nurse's experience with similar surgeries
questions.rationale:
The client's report of pain is the most reliable indicator, because pain is a personal experience shaped by biological, psychological, and social factors. The nurse accepts the report, treats the pain, and reassesses.

People cope with pain in different ways, so a calm expression or normal vital signs don't rule out severe pain. The nurse's experience with other clients doesn't measure this client's pain.

questions.stem: For each statement, click to specify whether it describes acute pain or chronic pain.
rows: Began recently, after an injury or surgery
Is associated with nerve changes from diabetes
Is expected to go away as the tissue heals
questions.rationale: Acute pain has a recent onset, after an injury or surgery, and serves a protective purpose: it warns of tissue damage and usually goes away as the tissue heals. Chronic pain persists, with ongoing tissue inflammation or changes in the peripheral nerves, as in arthritis, diabetes, or tumor growth.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about the pain experience. Which statements by the nurse are accurate?
options: Past experiences with pain can change how a person feels pain and responds to it.
The same injury causes the same amount of pain in everyone.
Culture and beliefs can shape how a person expresses pain.
A client who is laughing with visitors can't be in severe pain.
Support from family and friends can affect how a person copes with pain.
Anxiety can make pain feel worse.
questions.rationale:
Pain is biopsychosocial: biological, psychological, and social factors all shape it. Past experiences, culture and beliefs, anxiety, and support from others can all change how strongly pain is felt and how a person responds to it. That's why the client's own report is the most reliable indicator.

The same injury does not cause the same pain in everyone. People cope with pain in different ways, so a client laughing with visitors, which can be a distraction, may still be in severe pain.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching an older adult about sensory changes with aging. Which statement by the client shows understanding?
options: My sense of smell may weaken, so I'll keep my smoke detector working.
My hearing should get sharper as I age, so I won't need hearing tests.
Older adults always feel pain more strongly than younger adults do.
New glasses can fix any change in my vision that comes with age.
questions.rationale:
With aging, taste and smell often weaken, so safety measures such as a working smoke detector make sense, along with checking the dates on food. Older adults also commonly have reduced vision (cataracts, macular degeneration, glaucoma) and hearing loss.

Hearing usually declines with age: almost 1 in 4 adults aged 65 to 74, and 1 in 2 aged 75 and older, have disabling hearing loss, so hearing checks still matter. Pain doesn't always feel stronger with age; some older adults feel less pain, which can hide an injury. Age-related problems such as cataracts and glaucoma need treatment that glasses can't provide.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who has severely impaired vision. Which actions help the nurse communicate effectively?
options: Use hand gestures to show the client what to do.
Describe the layout of the room and where things are.
Explain what you are about to do before touching the client.
Move the client's belongings without saying so, to keep the room tidy.
Introduce yourself each time you enter the room.
questions.rationale:
For a client with impaired vision, the nurse says who they are each time they come in, describes the surroundings and where things are, and gives spoken explanations before and during care, so the client isn't startled and can stay independent.

Gestures don't help someone who can't see them. Moving belongings without telling the client takes away the client's sense of where things are and increases the risk of falls.

questions.stem: A pregnant client asks when the baby will first be able to recognize the mother's voice. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: Only after the baby is about 3 months old
Around 25 weeks of pregnancy, before birth
Not until the baby begins to speak
At birth, when the ears first fill with air
questions.rationale:
Many senses begin developing before birth. A fetus can recognize the mother's voice by about 25 weeks of pregnancy. Other milestones include swallowing (taste) at about 17 weeks, smelling odors at about 28 weeks, and pupils constricting to light at 30 to 32 weeks. Color vision develops around 3 months after birth.

Recognizing the voice doesn't wait until 3 months after birth (when color vision develops) or until the baby speaks. Hearing doesn't begin at birth; it develops in the womb.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that suggest the client has a hearing impairment.
questions.passage: Client [[asks the nurse to repeat several questions]] and [[leans toward the nurse while the nurse speaks]]. [[Denies ear pain, drainage, or dizziness]]. [[Watches the nurse's lips closely]]. States that at church dinners, [[people are talking, but the client can't make out what they're saying]]. [[Ear canals are clear]], and the [[tympanic membranes are intact and pearly gray]]. The granddaughter reports that the client [[often misses phone calls]] and [[keeps the television very loud]].
questions.rationale:
Signs of a hearing impairment are asking for questions to be repeated, leaning toward the speaker, and watching the speaker's lips, which suggests the client relies on lip reading. So are knowing that people are talking without understanding the words (worse with background noise), missing phone calls, and keeping the TV very loud.

No ear pain, drainage, or dizziness, clear ear canals, and intact, pearly gray tympanic membranes are normal findings. They point away from an infection or a cerumen blockage, which would cause a conductive hearing loss.

questions.stem: For each cause of hearing loss, click to specify whether it causes conductive or sensorineural hearing loss.
rows: Fluid in the middle ear from otitis media
Damage to the hair cells of the cochlea from years of loud noise
questions.rationale: Conductive hearing loss happens when sound can't reach the inner ear, as with cerumen blocking the ear canal or fluid in the middle ear from otitis media, which is common in young children. Sensorineural hearing loss comes from problems in the cochlea, the auditory nerve, or the brain, such as presbycusis, noise damage to the cochlea's hair cells, and Ménière disease. This client's clear ear canals and normal eardrums, with aging and years of loud machinery, fit a sensorineural loss.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse take to communicate effectively with the client?
options: Move to a quiet room away from background noise.
Turn away to type in the record while asking questions.
Shout so the client can hear every word.
Face the client and speak clearly at a normal pace.
Ask the client to repeat back the key points of any instructions.
Direct the questions to the granddaughter instead of the client.
questions.rationale:
The nurse should face the client and speak clearly, so the client can see the nurse's lips and expressions, reduce background noise, which makes speech harder to understand, and confirm understanding by asking the client to repeat back key points.

Shouting distorts speech and can feel disrespectful. Talking to the granddaughter instead of the client leaves the client out of their own care. Turning away to type hides the nurse's face and muffles the voice.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The client's findings are most consistent with {{0}}, a {{1}} hearing loss that affects {{2}}.

options: acute otitis media
presbycusis
cerumen impaction
conductive
sensorineural
both ears
only one ear

questions.rationale:
Hearing loss that has crept up over several years in an older adult, with trouble understanding words in noisy places, normal ear canals and eardrums, and a family history of hearing loss, fits presbycusis: a sensorineural, age-related hearing loss that affects both ears. Years of loud machinery may have added noise damage.

Acute otitis media would cause ear pain and fluid behind the eardrum, and cerumen impaction would block the canal; both cause conductive loss, and this client's canals and eardrums are normal. Presbycusis affects both ears, not only one.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the external ear. Which of the following is the function of the auricle (pinna)?
options: It catches sound waves and funnels them into the ear canal.
It amplifies vibrations and passes them to the inner ear.
It senses rotation of the head to help with balance.
It makes the cerumen that protects the ear canal.
questions.rationale:
The auricle (pinna), the visible outer ear, catches sound and funnels it into the external auditory canal, which leads to the eardrum.

The ossicles of the middle ear amplify vibrations and pass them to the inner ear. The semicircular canals of the inner ear sense rotation of the head. Cerumen (earwax) is made in the ear canal, not by the auricle.

Takeaway: The auricle catches and funnels sound; the canal makes cerumen.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the parts of the ear. For each structure, click to specify where it is.
questions.rationale:
The external ear is the auricle (pinna) and the external auditory canal, which catch sound and funnel it to the eardrum. The middle ear holds the tympanic membrane and the three ossicles, the malleus, incus, and stapes, which pass the vibration on and amplify it. The inner ear holds the cochlea, a fluid-filled, snail-shaped organ, and the organ of Corti, which sits on the cochlear tubes and turns fluid movement into nerve signals.

Takeaway: The external ear is the auricle and canal, the middle ear the eardrum and ossicles, and the inner ear the cochlea and organ of Corti.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching about hearing. Which of the following lobes of the brain processes the hearing signals carried by the vestibulocochlear nerve?
options: Occipital lobe
Temporal lobe
Frontal lobe
Parietal lobe
questions.rationale:
The cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) carries hearing signals to the temporal lobe, which handles auditory processing.

The occipital lobe processes vision, the frontal lobe handles movement, planning, and Broca's speech area, and the parietal lobe processes touch and body position.

Takeaway: Hearing is processed in the temporal lobe.

questions.stem: A client has hearing loss because many hair cells of the organ of Corti are damaged. Which of the following describes the problem?
options: Sound waves can't reach the eardrum through the ear canal.
The ossicles can't pass the vibration to the inner ear.
The eardrum can't vibrate in response to sound.
Fluid movement in the cochlea isn't turned into nerve signals.
questions.rationale:
The organ of Corti sits on the cochlear tubes, and its tiny hair cells bend as the cochlear fluid moves, creating the nerve signals that CN VIII carries to the brain. If the hair cells are damaged, sound can still reach the cochlea and move its fluid, but the movement isn't turned into nerve signals, so hearing is lost.

A blocked ear canal, ossicles that can't move, or an eardrum that can't vibrate are problems earlier in the path, before the sound reaches the cochlea.

Takeaway: The hair cells of the organ of Corti turn cochlear fluid movement into nerve signals.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the vestibular system. For each description, click to specify the structures it describes.
rows: Sense turning the head from side to side
Sense an elevator starting to go up
questions.rationale:
The semicircular canals are fluid-filled tubes lined with hair cells that sense rotary motion, motion that isn't in a straight line, such as turning or tilting the head. The utricle and saccule (the otolith organs, in the vestibule) contain hair cells and crystal-like otoconia, which shift with the fluid to sense straight-line movement: forward or backward (a car braking) and up or down (an elevator).

Takeaway: The semicircular canals sense turning; the utricle and saccule, with their otoconia, sense straight-line motion.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the nerves of the ear. Which of the following cranial nerves carries signals from the vestibular system to the brain?
options: Facial (CN VII)
Glossopharyngeal (CN IX)
Vestibulocochlear (CN VIII)
Trigeminal (CN V)
questions.rationale:
The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) has two branches: the vestibular branch carries head position and movement (balance), and the cochlear branch carries hearing.

The facial nerve (CN VII) controls facial expression, the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) serves the back of the tongue and the pharynx, and the trigeminal nerve (CN V) carries facial sensation and controls chewing.

Takeaway: CN VIII carries both balance (vestibular) and hearing (cochlear).

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing the hair cells of the semicircular canals with those of the cochlea. Which of the following describes the hair cells of the semicircular canals?
options: They react to fluid that moves with body movements, not with sound.
They react to sound waves that are passed on by the ossicles.
They react to light that reaches the inner ear through the canal.
They react to chemicals that are dissolved in the fluid of the ear.
questions.rationale:
Both the cochlea and the semicircular canals use hair cells bathed in fluid. In the cochlea, the fluid moves with sound waves. In the semicircular canals, the hair cells instead react to fluid that moves with body movements, especially turning or tilting the head, which is how they sense balance.

Sound waves passed on by the ossicles move the cochlear fluid, not the fluid of the semicircular canals. Light and dissolved chemicals are sensed by the eye and by the taste and smell receptors.

Takeaway: The cochlea's hair cells sense sound; the semicircular canals' hair cells sense body movement.

questions.stem: Click the clear structure at the front of the eye that bends light first as it enters the eye.
questions.alt: Side view of the eye with the front on the left: a clear dome at the front, the colored iris with an opening in the middle, a clear oval structure behind the opening, a jelly-filled chamber lined by layers at the back, a small yellow spot at the center of the back, and a thick nerve leaving the back of the eye.
questions.rationale:
The cornea, the clear dome at the front of the eye, is the eye's front window and bends (focuses) light first as it enters. An unevenly curved, egg-shaped cornea causes astigmatism.

The lens, behind the pupil, fine-tunes the focus; the macula, at the back, gives sharp central vision; and the optic nerve carries the signals to the brain.

Takeaway: The cornea bends light first; the lens fine-tunes the focus.

questions.stem: A client walks from a dark room into bright sunlight. Which of the following changes in the eye protects the retina from the extra light?
options: The lens becomes thicker and rounder.
The iris makes the pupil smaller.
The cornea becomes cloudy.
The rods take over from the cones.
questions.rationale:
The iris is the colored muscle that controls the size of the pupil, regulating how much light enters. In bright light the pupil constricts (gets smaller), letting in less light.

The lens changes shape to focus for near and far, not to control light. A cloudy cornea or lens is a disorder, not a response to light. Rods work in dim light, while cones handle bright light, color, and detail.

Takeaway: The iris controls the pupil: smaller in bright light, larger in dim light.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing eye assessments. For each test, click to specify what it checks.
questions.rationale:
The Snellen chart screens visual acuity, the sharpness of distance vision. Ishihara plates, circular plates of colored dots, screen for red–green color vision deficiency. The Amsler grid of horizontal and vertical lines monitors the central visual field, which macular degeneration damages. The refraction test checks how well the eyes focus light on the retina, to determine corrective lenses for myopia and hyperopia. Tonometry measures intraocular pressure, to check for glaucoma.

Takeaway: Snellen checks sharpness, Ishihara red and green, Amsler central vision, refraction the need for glasses, and tonometry eye pressure.

questions.stem: During a Snellen screening, the vision in a client's right eye is recorded as 20/40. Which of the following explains this result?
options: The client sees at 40 ft what a normal eye sees at 20 ft.
The client has 40% of normal vision in the right eye.
The client sees at 20 ft what a normal eye sees at 40 ft.
The client can read 20 of the 40 letters on the chart.
questions.rationale:
In a Snellen result, the top number is the client's distance from the chart, usually 20 ft, and the bottom number is the distance at which a normal eye can read that line. So 20/40 means the client sees at 20 ft what a normal eye sees at 40 ft: the client's distance vision is worse than normal.

Reversing the numbers would describe better-than-normal vision. The result isn't a percentage or a count of letters.

Takeaway: 20/40 means the client sees at 20 ft what a normal eye sees at 40 ft.

questions.stem: A client can't see the numbers hidden in several circular plates of colored dots. Which of the following conditions does this result suggest?
options: Glaucoma
Myopia
Macular degeneration
Color vision deficiency
questions.rationale:
The circular plates of colored dots are Ishihara plates (pseudoisochromatic plates). A number made of dots of one color hides among dots of another color, and a client with a red–green color vision deficiency can't pick it out.

Glaucoma is checked with tonometry, myopia with the Snellen chart and the refraction test, and macular degeneration with the Amsler grid.

Takeaway: Ishihara plates screen for red–green color vision deficiency.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client how to use an Amsler grid at home. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?
options: “Cover one eye, stare at the center dot, and report wavy or missing lines.”
“Stand 20 feet away, and read the smallest line of letters that you can see.”
“Look through each of the two lenses, and tell me which one looks clearer.”
“Find the number hidden among the colored dots on each of the round plates.”
questions.rationale:
The Amsler grid is a grid of horizontal and vertical lines with a center dot. The client covers one eye, stares at the center dot, and reports lines that look wavy, blurry, or missing, which suggest macular degeneration. Testing each eye regularly shows changes in central vision early.

Reading letters from 20 feet is the Snellen test, comparing lenses is the refraction test, and finding numbers among colored dots is the Ishihara test.

Takeaway: With the Amsler grid, test one eye at a time: stare at the dot, and report wavy or missing lines.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the needs of four clients at an eye clinic. Which client most needs tonometry?
options: A 30-year-old who can't read road signs clearly while driving
A 62-year-old with no symptoms whose mother had glaucoma
A 45-year-old who now holds books at arm's length to read
A 25-year-old who has trouble telling red from green
questions.rationale:
Tonometry measures intraocular pressure to check for glaucoma, which can damage vision before the person notices any symptoms. An older client with a family history of glaucoma and no symptoms is the one who most needs it.

Blurry road signs suggest myopia (Snellen chart and refraction), holding books at arm's length suggests presbyopia (reading glasses), and trouble telling red from green suggests a color vision deficiency (Ishihara plates).

Takeaway: Tonometry screens for glaucoma, which is silent at first, so risk factors decide who needs it.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing refractive errors and related eye findings. For each description, click to specify the condition it describes.
rows: Light focuses in front of the retina, so distant objects are blurry
The lens stiffens with age, so close objects are hard to focus on
The cornea or lens is egg-shaped, so vision is blurry at all distances
Light focuses behind the retina, so near objects are blurry
questions.rationale:
In myopia (nearsightedness), light focuses in front of the retina, so near is clear and far is blurry. In hyperopia (farsightedness), light focuses behind the retina, so far is clear and near is blurry. Presbyopia is age-related farsightedness: the lens stiffens, usually after 40, and can't focus up close. In astigmatism, the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped rather than round, so light focuses unevenly and vision is blurry or distorted at all distances.

Takeaway: Myopia blurs far vision, hyperopia and presbyopia blur near vision, and astigmatism blurs vision at all distances.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old client who has always had good vision now holds the menu at arm's length to read it, but sees road signs clearly. Which of the following explains this change?
options: Light is focusing in front of the retina because the eyeball is too long.
The cornea has become egg-shaped, which blurs vision at all distances.
The lens has stiffened with age and can't change shape for close focus.
The macula has been damaged, which causes a loss of central vision.
questions.rationale:
New trouble focusing up close after age 40, in someone who has always seen well, is presbyopia: the lens stiffens with age and can't change shape enough for near focus, so the client holds reading material farther away. Reading glasses help.

Light focusing in front of the retina is myopia, which blurs distant objects. An egg-shaped cornea (astigmatism) blurs vision at all distances. Damage to the macula (macular degeneration) causes a loss of central vision. Hyperopia also blurs near vision, but it comes from the shape of the eye, not aging of the lens.

Takeaway: Presbyopia and hyperopia both blur near vision; presbyopia comes from aging of the lens.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching about the sense of taste. Which of the following describes where the taste buds are found?
options: Inside the nasal cavity
In the salivary glands
On the teeth and gums
On the papillae of the tongue
questions.rationale:
Taste buds sit on the papillae, the small bumps of the tongue. Their receptor cells detect chemicals dissolved in saliva.

The nasal cavity holds the receptors for smell, which adds a great deal to flavor. The salivary glands make saliva, and taste isn't limited to the roof of the mouth.

Takeaway: Taste buds sit on the papillae of the tongue and detect chemicals dissolved in saliva.

questions.stem: A client whose mouth is very dry from a medication says that food tastes dull. Which of the following explanations by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Taste receptors detect chemicals dissolved in saliva, so dryness dulls taste.”
“A dry mouth damages the taste buds permanently, so this won't improve.”
“The medicine has blocked the nerve that carries smell from your nose.”
“Food tastes dull because the dry mouth has worn away the papillae.”
questions.rationale:
Taste receptor cells detect chemicals that are dissolved in saliva. With too little saliva, fewer flavor chemicals reach the receptors, so food tastes dull. Sips of water and treating the dry mouth can help.

A dry mouth doesn't usually damage the taste buds permanently. The medication's effect here is on saliva, not on the olfactory nerve (CN I), and the papillae are still there.

Takeaway: Taste needs saliva: chemicals must dissolve in it to reach the taste receptors.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching about interoception. Which of the following sensations are examples of interoception?
options: Feeling hungry before lunch
Knowing where the arm is with the eyes closed
Feeling the heart pounding after climbing stairs
Feeling the texture of a sweater
Sensing that the bladder is full
Feeling nauseated
questions.rationale:
Interoception is the sense of the body's internal state: hunger, thirst, the heartbeat, breathing, the need to urinate or have a bowel movement, and nausea.

Knowing where the arm is without looking is proprioception (body position), and feeling a sweater's texture is touch, sensed by the skin's mechanoreceptors.

Takeaway: Interoception is the inner sense of hunger, thirst, heartbeat, breathing, bladder, bowel, and nausea.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing proprioception. Which of the following receptors provide the sense of body position?
options: Rods and cones in the retina at the back of the eye
Receptors in the muscles, tendons, and joints
Taste buds on the papillae of the tongue
Hair cells in the cochlea of the inner ear
questions.rationale:
Proprioception is the sense of body position: where the body parts are in relation to each other, and the effort used to move them, without looking. Its receptors are in the muscles, tendons, and joints, and the signals are processed in the parietal lobe and the cerebellum.

Rods and cones sense light, taste buds sense dissolved chemicals, and the cochlea's hair cells sense sound.

Takeaway: Proprioception comes from receptors in the muscles, tendons, and joints.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the pathway for the sense of touch. Which of the following parts of the brain processes touch signals from the skin?
options: The occipital lobe
The temporal lobe
The parietal lobe
The frontal lobe
questions.rationale:
Touch is detected by the skin's mechanoreceptors (Merkel discs, Ruffini endings, and Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles) and by free nerve endings, and the signals are processed in the parietal lobe, which handles sensation and proprioception.

The occipital lobe processes vision, the temporal lobe hearing, and the frontal lobe movement, planning, and Broca's speech area.

Takeaway: Touch signals go to the parietal lobe.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing four clients. Which client's finding shows a problem with interoception?
options: A client who can't tell whether a toe is pointing up or down with the eyes closed
A client who can't feel the vibration of a tuning fork on the ankle
A client who can't identify a coin by touch with the eyes closed
A client who doesn't sense the need to urinate until the bladder overflows
questions.rationale:
Interoception is the sense of the body's internal state, including the need to urinate. Not sensing a full bladder until it overflows is a problem with interoception.

Not knowing a toe's position with the eyes closed is a problem with proprioception (body position). Not feeling a vibration, or not identifying a coin by touch, is a problem with touch: the skin's mechanoreceptors and their pathways.

Takeaway: Proprioception is body position; interoception is internal feelings such as hunger, thirst, and bladder fullness.

questions.stem: An older adult client reports that vision has become cloudy and dim, with bright glare from headlights at night. The nurse notes that the pupil looks cloudy. Which of the following conditions is most likely?
options: Myopia
Astigmatism
Glaucoma
Cataracts
questions.rationale:
Cataracts are clouding of the lens as its proteins break down. They cause cloudy, dim, blurry vision, glare (especially from headlights at night), and a cloudy-looking pupil.

Myopia blurs distant objects but doesn't cloud the lens, astigmatism blurs vision at all distances because of an egg-shaped cornea or lens, and glaucoma is high pressure in the eye, found with tonometry.

Takeaway: Cloudy, dim vision with glare and a cloudy pupil points to cataracts.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the receptors of the skin. Which of the following receptors detect pain and temperature?
options: Free nerve endings
Meissner corpuscles
Pacinian corpuscles
Merkel discs
questions.rationale:
Free nerve endings in the skin detect pain and temperature. Touch, pressure, vibration, and stretch are detected by the mechanoreceptors: Merkel discs (steady pressure and edges), Meissner corpuscles (fine touch and low-frequency vibration), Pacinian corpuscles (high-frequency vibration and pressure), and Ruffini endings (stretch).

Takeaway: Free nerve endings sense pain and temperature; the mechanoreceptors sense touch, pressure, vibration, and stretch.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' notes that need follow-up.
questions.passage: Client reports that [[straight lines, such as door frames, look wavy in the center when using the right eye]]. [[Holds the event program at arm's length to read it]]. [[Has not had an eye exam in 4 years]]. [[Denies eye pain]]. [[Eyes are clear, with no redness or drainage]]. [[Pupils are equal and react to light]].
questions.rationale:
Three findings need follow-up. Straight lines that look wavy in the center suggest damage to the macula (macular degeneration), which causes central vision loss. Holding reading material at arm's length suggests presbyopia, which reading glasses can correct. And a client who has had diabetes for 15 years without an eye exam in 4 years is overdue: diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) before symptoms appear, so yearly eye exams are needed.

No eye pain, clear eyes without redness or drainage, and equal pupils that react to light are expected findings.

Takeaway: Wavy central lines, new trouble reading up close, and missed yearly eye exams in diabetes all need follow-up.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The wavy lines on the Amsler grid suggest {{0}}, and holding reading material at arm's length suggests {{1}}.

options: cataracts
macular degeneration
glaucoma
myopia
astigmatism
presbyopia

questions.rationale:
The Amsler grid monitors the central visual field, so wavy lines and a blurry spot near the center suggest macular degeneration, damage to the macula, usually related to age. Holding reading material at arm's length after age 40 suggests presbyopia, the age-related stiffening of the lens.

Cataracts cause cloudy, dim vision with glare. Glaucoma is found with tonometry, and this client's eye pressure is normal. Myopia blurs distant objects, and astigmatism blurs vision at all distances.

Takeaway: Wavy central lines point to macular degeneration; near-vision trouble after 40 points to presbyopia.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings needs the most prompt referral to an eye provider?
options: The new wavy lines and blurry spot in the right eye
Holding the event program at arm's length to read it
The normal results of the Ishihara color plates
The normal eye pressure on tonometry
questions.rationale:
New wavy lines and a blurry spot in central vision suggest macular degeneration, which can progress to a loss of central vision. A new change like this needs prompt evaluation by an eye provider.

Trouble reading up close (presbyopia) is common after 40 and is corrected with reading glasses; it isn't urgent. Normal Ishihara plates and normal eye pressure are reassuring findings, not reasons for referral.

Takeaway: A new change in central vision needs prompt follow-up; presbyopia can wait for routine care.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the client's tonometry result show?
options: The client's central vision is normal in both eyes.
The eye pressure is normal, with no sign of glaucoma.
The client's red–green color vision is normal.
The client doesn't need glasses for distance vision.
questions.rationale:
Tonometry measures the pressure inside the eye (intraocular pressure) to check for glaucoma. A normal result means the eye pressure is normal, with no sign of glaucoma at this time.

Central vision is checked with the Amsler grid, and this client's is abnormal in the right eye. Color vision is checked with the Ishihara plates, and the need for corrective lenses with the refraction test.

Takeaway: Tonometry measures eye pressure for glaucoma, and nothing else.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches the client about diabetic retinopathy. Which of the following statements by the client shows an understanding of the teaching?
options: “I'll wait to have an eye exam until I notice my vision getting worse.”
“Diabetes can affect my feet and kidneys, but it doesn't affect my eyes.”
“I need a yearly eye exam, since diabetes can harm my retina without symptoms.”
“My eyes are healthy, because my color vision test today was normal.”
questions.rationale:
In diabetic retinopathy, chronic high blood glucose damages the small blood vessels of the retina. There are no symptoms at first; later come blurred vision and, without treatment, blindness. That is why people with diabetes need yearly eye exams.

Waiting for symptoms misses the early, treatable stage. Diabetes does affect the eyes, as well as the feet and kidneys. A normal color vision test doesn't show the health of the retina's blood vessels.

Takeaway: Diabetic retinopathy is silent at first, so clients with diabetes need an eye exam every year.
